head: 8391608c8d772574bbefe69c712cc817c466ce90
body:
Extending the coverage subtraction from `src` to `api` and the process entry points found two more things nothing executed.

## `server.mjs` — 614 lines, 87 branches, zero gates

The largest coverage hole here, and it stayed open for a structural reason rather than neglect: the handler is an inline anonymous function, and importing the module runs `validateStartupConfig`, creates a store, `await`s `store.init()` and can start a scheduler. **Nothing could reach the routing logic without a running process, so nothing did.**

So the gate runs the process. It spawns the real server on loopback with a throwaway JSON store and `PROCESS_ROLE=web` — the same code production runs, minus the scheduler. Every URL is `127.0.0.1`; no external request is made.

What is now proven, none of which was before:

- **16 admin routes** each refuse an anonymous caller with 401
- each refuses a wrong token, a token with a suffix, a truncated token, and the raw token without the `Bearer` scheme — **64 combinations**
- the public routes are public, and the list of them is short
- **all five security headers** reach the client on public, refused *and* 404 responses alike
- a 404 carries no stack trace or internal path
- a refusal never echoes the expected token

### On the ordering

This is a smoke gate, **not** a substitute for extracting the handler. Extraction is still worth doing — it would make those 87 branches individually testable instead of only reachable through a socket.

But extracting is a real refactor of the main HTTP surface, and doing it with no gate to catch a mistake is how you break production. A running gate today is worth more than a refactor with nothing to check it. **That ordering was the whole judgement here**, and the extraction should now be done under this net.

## The admin health route

One finding, and it needs an honest severity. `equalBearer` coerced with `String(header||'')`, so an object whose `toString` returned the right bearer was admitted.

**This is not a live bypass.** Over HTTP a header is only a string or an array of strings; an attacker cannot supply an object. It is fixed because the coercion was doing work nobody asked for, and because `src/agent-mesh-cron-boundary.mjs` already had the right shape one file over — normalize to a string or empty, and refuse a non-string outright rather than by accident.

The route otherwise held: configuration is checked before the secret, so an unconfigured route cannot be used to learn whether the secret was wrong; a failing read is 503 and never a healthy matrix; the driver's error text and internal host stay out of the response.

A second thing I reported was **my own test being wrong** — a lowercase `get` is served, deliberately, consistently with the cron boundary. Pinned as a choice rather than left looking like an oversight.

- The mutation sandbox copied `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `config`, `migrations` and (as of #235) `api`, but **not `server.mjs` or `worker.mjs`** — so a mutation of either could not have meant anything.
- The coverage ratchet counted only **imports**, so it reported a spawned entry point as uncovered. Executing a module by spawning it is still executing it.

title: Close the two production paths no gate executed, and ratchet the gap shut
head: 2e0c11baaed3e7664a26ae982f0394cc4ebe5af8
body:
The reachability ratchet answers *"can anything call this module?"*. The question underneath it — ***"does anything check it?"*** — had never been asked.

Taking the closure of everything the gates import and subtracting it from the production-reachable set found exactly two modules that a live route reaches and no gate runs:

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `src/database-hygiene-repository.mjs` | **DELETES rows** on a weekly cron |
| `src/discovery-runner.mjs` | decides whether discovery may run at all |

That combination has already cost this repository once, this week: the browser crawler shipped a `ReferenceError` on every call because its only real gate had been written off as blocked.

**A DELETE on a schedule is the worst thing to leave in that set** — not because the code was wrong (it survived every attack unchanged) but because nothing would have noticed if it stopped being right.

## What the hygiene attack proved

Against a real database: an unexpired cache row survives; an expired row written today survives the `updated_at` guard; `READY` and `CLAIMED` staged content survive while only terminal content past retention is taken; a **400-day-old `payment_classification` receipt is untouched**; batch size clamps in both directions; and a retention value that is not a number **fails the run rather than guessing a cutoff**.

At the route: `MAINTENANCE_ENABLED` absent, `"false"`, `"1"` and `"yes"` all delete nothing. A wrong secret, a missing schedule header and a POST delete nothing **even with maintenance enabled**.

### Two of my own errors, recorded

My throwaway attack script wrapped the audit-log insert in a `catch`, so its "money survives" check passed **vacuously** on a row that was never created. The permanent test caught it by failing on a NOT NULL column — which is the argument for writing the permanent test rather than trusting the scratch one.

I also asserted 401 for a missing schedule header. The boundary correctly answers **403**: a bad secret is unauthenticated, a bad schedule is an authenticated caller asking for something the route does not serve.

## What the discovery attack proved

Every refusal happens **before any Overpass request**, so the guards are proven with zero external I/O. An unknown campaign, an unapproved campaign, a missing bounding box and an exhausted daily cap each refuse, record the failure on the run, log it, and mark the error non-retryable so a scheduler cannot retry it forever.

No option — `scheduled`, `limit`, `dryRun`, an explicit bbox — substitutes for approval. An errored run does not burn the day's quota. And a dry run **is not effect-free**: it still reaches Overpass, it only declines to import. The test says so plainly, because reading `dryRun` as "makes no request" would be wrong.

## The ratchet

`tests/production-coverage-ratchet.test.mjs` keeps the uncovered set empty without anyone re-running that analysis, and asserts its own two halves are non-trivial — a subtraction over derived sets is easy to make vacuously true by widening what counts as a gate.

Deliberately **not** a coverage percentage. Line coverage measures how much of a module ran; this measures whether anything runs it at all, which is a weaker claim and a much harder one to argue with.

The mutation sandbox copied `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, `config` and `migrations` but **not `api`** — so no route could be mutated at all, and a mutation naming one failed with `ENOENT` rather than reporting a surviving guard. Routes are where admission and enablement checks live.

| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |

head: 5ec9092c74b358924b34ab3cd38326e831403d3a
body:
Two defects, both on the path from a paid webhook to someone knowing about it.

## P1 — verified payment evidence accumulated where nobody could see it

`api/webhooks/billing.mjs` writes a row into `billing_webhook_inbox` for every verified delivery. **Nothing in this tree reads those rows.** `claimBillingEvents`, `finishBillingEvent`, `billingBacklogSummary` and `planPaymentReconciliation` have no callers anywhere in `src`, `api`, `scripts`, `server.mjs` or `worker.mjs`.

So evidence about money arrives, is stored, and is never claimed, retried, timed out, dead-lettered, or mentioned to anyone.

**This is not closed by writing a reconciliation worker.** There is no payment provider to reconcile against, and a worker that resolves nothing would be machinery pretending to be a capability. What *can* be closed with no external activation is the silence.

The operator health matrix now carries a billing dimension with four states, because one "pending" number would blur the fact that matters most:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `NOT_OBSERVED` | the query returned nothing — **not** the same as zero |
| `NO_WORKER` | evidence is waiting and nothing has **ever** claimed a row |
| `BACKLOG_AGEING` | a worker exists and unsettled evidence is past the threshold |
| `HEALTHY` | nothing unsettled, or nothing late |

`NO_WORKER` and `BACKLOG_AGEING` look identical in a counter and are not the same operational fact: **one resolves itself, the other never will.** `everClaimed` separates them, and `BILL-03` replaces it with a literal zero to prove that distinction is real rather than incidental.

Today the real query answers `NO_WORKER`, and the matrix reports the system `DEGRADED` for it — proven against a real database, not asserted.

No route change was needed: `api/admin/health-check.mjs` already spreads the repository output into the matrix, so the smallest bridge was to widen the query and the compiler and nothing else.

The rows summarized carry a provider event key, a payload hash and a recipient address in `custom_data`. A test asserts none of them reach the response, **against a real database with a real address seeded into the row.**

## P2 — the deterministic gate changed its answer based on the invoking shell

Running `npm run test:deterministic` from a shell with `OMNIA_V9_TEST_DATABASE_URL` exported turned a green gate red:

```
not ok - property run: 1000 deterministic crash/outcome/restart scenarios, zero duplicate external effects
```

The suite passes in isolation. Most database suites are not on the runner's exclusion list; they stay in the deterministic set and self-skip when the URL is absent. Export it and they execute there instead — **in parallel, sharing one database**, which is precisely the interference `run-real-postgres-tests.mjs` runs serially to avoid and says so in its own header.

A gate that fails for a reason unrelated to the code is the most expensive kind of red: it costs a diagnosis every time, and it teaches people that red might not mean anything.

The runner now drops the variable for its children. Verified both ways: **2808 tests, 2760 pass, 0 fail, 48 skipped — identical with and without the variable set.** Real database coverage is not lost; that is what `test:postgres-real` is for, serially.

### A wrong first attempt, kept in the record

I first made the deterministic exclusion derive from `realPostgresTestFiles()`, reasoning the two runners shouldn't disagree about what a database suite is. But that function discovers by *marker* — any file mentioning the variable — and many `omnia-v9-*` suites mention it only to decide whether to skip one case. Using it as an exclusion dropped roughly **128 genuinely deterministic tests**, 2807 → 2679.

The marker is correct for deciding what the PostgreSQL runner should **include** and wrong for deciding what the deterministic runner should **exclude**. Two `build-wiring` tests caught it immediately, which is what they are for.

| `test:browser` | 1/1 |
| `test:mutation-war` | **81 mutations, 81 killed** |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

`BILL-01` makes the degraded condition unconditional-false, `BILL-02` turns an unobserved dimension back into a healthy zero, `BILL-03` flattens `everClaimed`, `GATE-01` removes the environment deletion. All killed.

No customers, no cleared revenue, no accepted deliveries, no deployment. No provider was called, no message sent, no money moved. title: Integrate #231 and #230, and repair a P0 the browser gate caught
head: 225e76afcd0a8a21833cad77dcec111534095df6
body:
Reconciles the five open NIGHTFALL hardening PRs into one integration, after attacking what they add.

**#231 is an exact consolidation of #227, #228 and #229** — every source file verified byte-identical to the individual PR by hash before merging — so it is integrated once here and **#227, #228 and #229 should be closed as superseded**, not merged again. #230 is independent; its migration 103 does not collide with #231's 102.

## P0 — the browser crawler threw on every call

The pool integration moved the crawl result variables inside the `try` while the `return` stayed below the `finally`:

```
ReferenceError: pages is not defined
```

That is a total failure of the website-audit path, which is the product.

**It passed every gate except one.** `check:syntax` parses it. The deterministic suite does not cover the browser gate. The pool's own unit tests pass because they mock the browser. Only `npm run test:browser` against a real Chromium sees it — the gate that was recorded as permanently `BLOCKED_EXTERNAL_TEST_RUNTIME` until last shift proved Chromium was present all along. Had it stayed written off, this ships.

`CRAWL-01` mutates the declaration back inside the `try` and is killed.

## P1 — a duplicate webhook answered 503, and misstated why

The insert's `ON CONFLICT` named `provider_event_key`, correct when that was the only unique index. Migration 101 added a second on the content — `(provider, event_name, object_type, object_id, payload_hash)` — and a targeted clause does not cover it, so a provider redelivering identical content under a new event id raised `23505`. The route catches everything and answers 503 `verified-webhook-not-durably-persisted`.

That is both an outage and a false statement: the evidence **is** durably persisted, in the row being duplicated. Providers retry 503s and disable endpoints that keep failing, so a duplicate could cost the future events that are *not* duplicates.

Inherited from main — the clause is byte-identical on both sides, so #231 did not introduce it. `MONEY-17` restores the targeted form and is killed by a real-PostgreSQL test, because which index PostgreSQL raises on is not something a fake can prove.

## What survived attack unchanged

The lease itself, against real PostgreSQL: a crashed worker's lease is reclaimable rather than stranded; a preempted worker **cannot** finish; the attempt cap lands in `UNCERTAIN` for review and never promotes money or sets `completed_at`; `RECONCILED` without a canonical receipt throws; concurrent claims never hand one event to two workers; `RETRYABLE` honours its backoff; the backlog summary carries no key or payload.

Overpass stops at **one call** on 403/401/451/418/404 and retries only 429/406/504, honouring `Retry-After` and clamping an absurd value to 120s. The pool leaks no slot on launch failure, does not double-free, and rejects waiters on close rather than hanging them. The artifact boundary is fail-closed on every truthiness variant, cannot escape its namespace, and returns PRIVATE regardless of input.

## Two registry defects fixed along the way

`MONEY-13` and `MONEY-14` were **both** already taken, so a new mutation collided twice in a row and the war printed two lines under one id — ambiguous in the one place it must not be. There is now a uniqueness test and a malformedness test. The war also gained a `needsBrowser` gate mirroring `needsPostgres`, so a browser-dependent mutation reports `SKIPPED_NEEDS_BROWSER` rather than counting as killed when no browser is configured.

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `check:syntax` | 609 files parse |
| `test:deterministic` | 2798 tests, 2750 pass, **0 fail**, 48 skipped |
| `test:relay-safety` | 150/150 |
| `test:postgres-real` | **132/132** against PostgreSQL 16.13 |
| `test:browser` | 1/1 against the installed Chromium |
| `test:mutation-war` | **77 mutations, 77 killed**, with both a real database and a real browser |
| `npm audit --omit=dev` | 0 vulnerabilities |

The runner was rebuilt and no longer ships the PostgreSQL 18 binaries the previous receipt named. A fresh PostgreSQL 16.13 cluster was initialized locally; the receipt says 16.13 rather than carrying 18 forward, because the version is part of what the evidence means.

## One thing recorded rather than fixed

The artifact contract's sensitive-metadata-key check is top-level only, so `{outer:{api_key}}` is accepted. It leaks nothing — metadata never reaches the plan at all — so the check is a refusal signal, not a redaction. Noted so nobody later relies on it as a filter.

body:
## The sweep

The send-loop fix in #215 was one instance of a shape. This is the sweep for the rest: for every protected module that exports a decision, find the callers that can discard that decision while the deciding module stays untouched.

Five more, each **confirmed accepted** by the contract before being closed:

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `agent-code-change-applier.mjs` | Calls `validateAgentCodeChangeSet`, then writes files to disk |
| `agent-code-artifact-store.mjs` | Refuses to persist a change set that does not validate |
| `agent-git-sandbox-collector.mjs` | Compiles an agent's sandbox git diff into a change set — where a protected path is *first* refused |
| `agent-autonomy-pump.mjs` | Acts on `evaluateWorkerResultTruth` |
| `ai-employee-relay.mjs` | Acts on `evaluateWorkerResultTruth` |

`agent-code-change-contract.mjs` was protected as *"the rules about changing files, including this list"* — but the rules are enforced somewhere else, and that somewhere else was editable.

## Honest severity

The applier bypass is **two steps, not one**: a weakened applier only takes effect once merged and used by a later run, and it writes under a sandbox root with escape checking. But the second step is unbounded, and self-modification of the enforcement surface is the precise thing the list exists to prevent.

A false TERMINAL from a discarded truth decision is not an external effect either. It is the claim every downstream receipt is built on.

## Why both truth call sites had to close together

Each is the other's excuse. *"Avoid re-evaluating truth that the other one already checked"* is a plausible rationale for removing either, and removing both leaves nothing. A test asserts both stay protected for exactly this reason.

## The collector was not on my list

The test found it. It derives the rule from the import graph instead of trusting a list maintained by hand — the **second time in this session** the derived form caught something the manual form missed (the first was `server.mjs` and `store.mjs` being wrongly flagged in #215, which sharpened the rule from "imports a guard" to "asks for a decision").

That is the argument for writing them this way, and it is why this test also asserts that its own rule still fires: a check that cannot catch anything is worse than no check.
